title: The Lie That Dresses Like Scripture: How Lust Twists God’s Word to Justify Polygamy
paragraphs: The Lie That Dresses Like Scripture: How Lust Twists God’s Word to Justify Polygamy
There are sins that shout, and there are sins that whisper… and the most dangerous ones are the ones that learn how to quote Scripture while they’re whispering.

You’ve probably heard it before. Maybe you’ve even wrestled with it in silence. Someone opens the Bible, points to Abraham, David, Solomon… and suddenly what God tolerated in broken men is being preached as something He designed for holy living. And if we’re honest, sometimes the argument doesn’t come from a pulpit. It comes from a place deeper. Quieter. A place inside the human heart that doesn’t want to surrender desire… it wants to baptize it.
That’s where lust becomes a theologian.
Not a loud one. Not an obvious one. But a clever one.
The kind that doesn’t deny God’s Word… it twists it.

In the beginning, before kings, before kingdoms, before culture complicated everything, God already spoke clearly. In Genesis 2:24, the Hebrew is painfully simple, almost offensively direct to human desire: “וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד” (ve’hayu le’basar echad) — “and they shall become one flesh.”
Not one man and many women. Not divided flesh. Not shared covenant.
One.

There’s something sacred about that word in Hebrew — “אֶחָד” (echad). It doesn’t just mean one as a number. It means unity. Wholeness. Undivided existence. God wasn’t just defining marriage… He was revealing His own nature through it. A covenant that reflects divine faithfulness, not human appetite.
But lust doesn’t like “one.”
Lust wants more.
And when desire grows louder than devotion, people don’t usually abandon Scripture… they reinterpret it.

They point to Abraham and say, “But he had Hagar.”
They point to David and say, “But he had many wives.”
They point to Solomon and say, “But God still used him.”
What they don’t say… is what those choices cost.

Abraham’s house was torn by jealousy and exile.
David’s family was fractured by violence, betrayal, and grief.
Solomon’s heart was turned away from God, exactly as warned.
The Bible never hides the consequences. It records them in painful detail. Because Scripture is not endorsing their choices… it is exposing them.
There’s a difference between description and prescription. And lust depends on people confusing the two.
Jesus doesn’t leave room for confusion.

When questioned about marriage, He didn’t point to David or Solomon. He went all the way back. Back before sin complicated relationships. Back before culture normalized compromise. Back to the original design.
In Matthew 19:4–6, He says, “ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς” (ap’ archēs) — “from the beginning.”
Not from tradition. Not from cultural practice. Not from what people got away with.
From the beginning.
And then He repeats it: “the two shall become one flesh.”
Two.
Not three. Not many.
Two.
And then He says something that should shake every argument built on convenience: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Lust hears that… and still tries to negotiate.
Because lust isn’t just about desire for bodies. It’s about control. It’s about refusing to die to self. It’s about reshaping truth until it no longer confronts us.

Even the New Testament closes the door firmly. When describing church leadership in 1 Timothy 3:2, Paul writes that an overseer must be “μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα” (mias gynaikos andra) — literally, “a one-woman man.”
Not because faithfulness is optional for others… but because leadership must reflect what God already established as holy.
So why do people still argue for polygamy?
Because the heart is capable of reading truth… and still choosing desire.
And that’s the part no one likes to admit.
This isn’t just about ancient cultures or theological debates. This is about something personal. Something uncomfortable. Something that might be sitting quietly in your own thoughts.
Are there areas where you’re not rejecting God’s Word… you’re just reshaping it to fit what you want?
Be honest.
Because this is where the Gospel becomes more than information… it becomes confrontation.
Jesus didn’t come just to forgive sin. He came to destroy its authority.
Lust doesn’t get healed by justification. It gets healed by surrender.
And surrender feels like loss… until you realize what you’re actually gaining.
Freedom.
Clarity.
Wholeness.
The kind of love that isn’t divided, negotiated, or secretly compromised.
This is what grace does. It doesn’t adjust truth to fit your life… it transforms your life to align with truth.
And that transformation always starts the same way.
Honesty.
Sit with it.
Let it expose something if it needs to.
There’s no shame in admitting the struggle… but there is danger in pretending it’s not there.
And if this spoke to something real in you, don’t keep it to yourself. Someone close to you is quietly believing a lie that sounds biblical. Not to shame them… but to wake them up.
You’re going to need this reminder again when your feelings try to rewrite truth.
And follow closely, because truth like this isn’t something you hear once… it’s something you stay anchored to.
Not because truth is for sale… but because building something that reaches souls requires people who are willing to stand behind it.
If you truly want to glorify God, don’t just consume truth… help carry it.
Because someone out there is still believing a lie… and your share might be the moment it breaks.
The most dangerous deception isn’t rejecting God’s Word… it’s reshaping it until it no longer requires you to change.
